title: Your Childhood Isn't Your Children's Destiny
author: Be a Super Dad
summary: Prompted by a viral video in which a father stands still while his three children physically step forward for every positive childhood experience he apparently didn't receive, the Be a Super Dad newsletter explores how a father's own upbringing shapes, without permanently dictating, the parenting he offers his children. The author's central argument is that every parent arrives at parenthood having absorbed a set of unspoken lessons about affection, apology, anger, and safety long before being old enough to evaluate whether they agreed with them, and that this inheritance continues to surface involuntarily (hearing a parent's exact words come out of one's own mouth in moments of exhaustion). Rather than treating the video's father as either villain or simple triumph, the piece complicates the "breaking the cycle" narrative that dominates popular parenting discourse, arguing that knowing what not to repeat is not the same as knowing what to do instead, and that new parenting behaviors have to be actively learned, often by watching other parents, rather than willed into existence through good intentions alone. The essay widens the frame by noting the father's own formation likely drew on multiple influences beyond his father, mothers, grandparents, teachers, and coaches, arguing childhood shaping is messier and more hopeful than a single inherited blueprint. It closes by turning the lens back on the reader, inviting fathers to honestly examine what it is actually like to be parented by them right now, while their own children's story is still being written.
points: Uses a viral video's step-forward exercise to reframe intergenerational parenting change not as villain-versus-hero but as evidence that unspoken childhood lessons can be absorbed without becoming a fixed destiny for the next generation.

Argues most parenting lessons are absorbed nonverbally and pre-rationally in childhood, which explains why exhausted or angry parents sometimes hear their own parent's exact words come out of their mouth despite consciously rejecting them.

Complicates the popular "breaking the cycle" narrative by distinguishing knowing what not to repeat from actually knowing what to do instead, arguing the second, harder step requires active learning, not just good intentions.

Widens the model of formative influence beyond a single father figure, naming mothers, grandparents, teachers, coaches, and youth workers as sources that can each contribute one usable piece of the parent someone becomes.

Closes by redirecting the reflective exercise onto the reader's present parenting, asking what it is actually like to be around them when patience runs low, framed as a hopeful question precisely because a child's experience "isn't finished" yet.
quotes: A man who appears not to have received some of these things from his own dad has somehow managed to give them to his children.

Most of those lessons weren't taught to us in words, nobody sat there and explained them to us. They were simply happening around us while we were growing up, and we absorbed them, we felt them, before we were old enough to think very much about whether we agreed with them.
You can be absolutely certain that you'll never speak to your children the way somebody spoke to you and then, when you're exhausted and angry, hear a familiar sentence coming out of your own mouth.
Your childhood can influence the way you parent without becoming the childhood your own children are destined to have.
If nobody apologised in your house when you were growing up, where were you supposed to learn how to apologise to a child? Telling ourselves what we won't do can only take us so far.
There is hope in being able to ask those questions while our children are still growing up. Their experience of us isn't finished. Neither are we.
